title: Parameterized Queries and Security
description: Use SqlParameter to build safe, efficient queries and prevent SQL injection attacks.

data.text: Security is critical when building data access code. The most common vulnerability in database applications is **SQL Injection**, which occurs when untrusted user input is concatenated directly into a SQL string. **Parameterized queries** eliminate this risk by separating the SQL command structure from the data values.
Never build SQL queries by concatenating strings. An attacker can supply input that changes the meaning of your query, potentially reading, modifying, or deleting data they should not access.

data.title: SQL Injection example
data.text: If a user enters `'; DROP TABLE Inventory; --` into a search box and you concatenate it into SQL, the database may execute the DROP TABLE command. Parameterized queries prevent this entirely.

data.title: Vulnerable Code (DO NOT USE)
data.content: This pattern is extremely dangerous and must never be used.

data.text: **SqlParameter** objects represent values in a parameterized query. The database receives the SQL structure and the parameter values separately, so user input can never be interpreted as SQL code.

data.title: Safe Parameterized Query
data.content: Use parameters to safely pass user input to the database.

terms.definition: A security vulnerability where untrusted input alters the structure of a SQL query.
A SQL query that uses placeholders (@param) for values, with values provided separately as parameters.

data.text: `AddWithValue` infers the SQL type from the .NET type, which can sometimes lead to suboptimal query plans. For production code, explicitly set the `SqlDbType` when the type matters.

data.title: Explicit Parameter Types
data.content: Specify SqlDbType for precise type mapping.

data.text: A **stored procedure** is a batch of SQL statements stored in the database. Using stored procedures with ADO.NET provides benefits like execution plan reuse, reduced network traffic, and an extra layer of security.

data.text: Best Practices for Secure Data Access

items: Always use parameterized queries for user-supplied values.
Never concatenate user input into SQL strings.
Use `using` statements to ensure connections and commands are disposed.
Validate input on the server side, even if client-side validation exists.
Apply the principle of least privilege to database accounts.
Use output parameters sparingly and validate their values.

data.title: Exercise: Secure the Search Feature
data.description: Convert a vulnerable search feature into a secure parameterized query.
steps: Create a search form that accepts a product name.
Write the vulnerable concatenation-based query (for demonstration only).
Rewrite the query using SqlParameter with @Name.
Add a second filter for minimum price using @MinPrice.
Verify that entering SQL special characters like ' OR 1=1 -- returns no results.
data.expectedOutcome: You can write parameterized queries that safely handle any user input without SQL injection risk.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Never concatenate user input into SQL strings.
SqlParameter separates code from data, preventing SQL injection.
Stored procedures offer performance and security benefits.
Always validate input on the server side.
data.takeaway: Secure data access is not optional. Parameterized queries are the single most important defense against SQL injection in ADO.NET.
